name: SpQR (Sparse-Quantized Representation for near-lossless 3-4 bit compression)
bits: w4a16 (3-4 bits per weight with sparse outlier preservation)
activation_scheme: FP16 activations, no quantization. Weights are quantized to 3-4 bits with per-group scales, but outlier weights (those causing large quantization error) are stored in higher precision (FP16) in a sparse format.
kernels: SpQR GPU inference algorithm (custom CUDA kernels)
quality_delta: From the paper abstract: 'relative accuracy losses of less than 1% in perplexity for highly-accurate LLaMA and Falcon LLMs' at 3-4 bits per parameter. This is a stronger claim than GPTQ or AWQ make for the same bit width. The paper also reports '15% speedup' and 'memory compression gains of more than 4x' for a 33B parameter LLM on a single 24 GB consumer GPU. The <1% perplexity loss is the key differentiator: GPTQ at 4-bit typically shows 0.1-0.3 perplexity increase on Llama2-7B (see gptq record), which is already quite good, but SpQR claims to be near-lossless even at 3-bit.
notes:
PROXY ENUM VALUE - DECLARED 2026-10-04: SpQR is a quantization METHOD (sparse outlier preservation), not a format or a GPTQ variant. Filed under 'gptq' because both are grouped weight-only PTQ over the same grid and SpQR ships custom CUDA kernels. Nothing here misrepresents SpQR's target - it is a weight format, never KV or activation - but the enum makes a method queryable as if it were a storage format. REQUESTED ENUM ADDITION: 'spqr'. SpQR is a weight-only quantization method that specifically targets the outlier problem. The key insight is that most weights can be quantized to 3-4 bits with small error, but a small fraction of outlier weights cause disproportionately large errors. SpQR isolates these outliers and stores them in FP16 in a sparse format, while compressing all other weights to 3-4 bits. This is conceptually similar to SpQR's contemporary Atom (which also isolates outliers) but uses a different sparse encoding. The <1% perplexity loss claim is significant because it suggests that with proper outlier handling, 3-bit weight-only quantization can be nearly lossless. This is relevant to the repo's theme of silent failures: SpQR's approach makes the outlier problem explicit and visible, rather than letting it silently degrade quality. The paper is by Dettmers et al. (arXiv:2306.03078), who also created GPTQ, so SpQR can be seen as an evolution of GPTQ that adds explicit outlier handling. The 15% speedup is modest because the sparse outlier storage adds overhead - this is a case where the accuracy improvement comes at a small speed cost.
NATIVE_SUPPORT CLASSIFIED 2026-10-04: this field is still [] and that is CORRECT, but the empty list used to be ambiguous between three different states and now is not. Reason class on this record: WEIGHT-ONLY, SO STRUCTURALLY ABSENT. The bits field keeps activations in FP16, so execution is dequantize-to-FP16 then an FP16 tensor-core GEMM; there is no INT4-x-INT4 (or sub-8-bit x sub-8-bit) silicon instruction for it to target. This is a statement about the arithmetic, not an absence of investigation. Consequence for a reader: nothing further to verify - no silicon path is possible for this format as defined. The full statement of the three-way distinction, and the worked list of all 72 empty records by class, is in gotcha quant-native-support-empty-means-three-different-things. Rule of thumb for this field everywhere in the repo: if the bits field carries an 'a16', or the scheme is KV-cache-only or a llama.cpp integer storage type, an empty native_support is a DEFINITION and needs no verification; only a W4A4/W8A8/sub-8-bit format with research kernels can have an empty list that is a real finding.
